{{Distinguish|text=[[Kernel principal component analysis]] or [[Kernel method|Kernel ridge regression]]}}
{{short description|Technique in statistics}}
In [[statistics]], '''kernel regression''' is a [[non-parametric]] technique to estimate the [[conditional expectation]] of a [[random variable]]. The objective is to find a non-linear relation between a pair of random variables '''''X''''' and '''''Y'''''.

In any [[nonparametric regression]], the [[conditional expectation]] of a variable <math>Y</math> relative to a variable <math>X</math> may be written:

: <math>\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X) = m(X)</math>

where <math>m</math> is an unknown function.

== Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression ==
[[Èlizbar Nadaraya|Nadaraya]] and [[Geoffrey Watson|Watson]], both in 1964, proposed to estimate <math>m</math> as a locally weighted average, using a [[kernel (statistics)|kernel]] as a weighting function.<ref>{{cite journal
  | last = Nadaraya
  | first = E. A.
  | title = On Estimating Regression
  | journal = Theory of Probability and Its Applications
  | volume = 9
  | issue = 1
  | pages = 141–2
  | year = 1964
  | doi = 10.1137/1109020 
  }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=G. S. |last=Watson |title=Smooth regression analysis |journal=Sankhyā: The Indian Journal of Statistics, Series A |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=359–372 |year=1964 |jstor=25049340 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=Herman J. |last=Bierens |title=Topics in Advanced Econometrics |url=https://archive.org/details/topicsinadvanced0000bier |location=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1994 |isbn=0-521-41900-X |chapter=The Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression function estimator |pages=[https://archive.org/details/topicsinadvanced0000bier/page/n227 212]–247 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M5QBuJVtbWQC&pg=PA212 }}</ref> The Nadaraya–Watson estimator is:

: <math> \widehat{m}_h(x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i) y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^nK_h(x-x_i)}
</math>

where <math>K_h(t) = \frac{1}{h}K\left(\frac{t}{h}\right)</math> is a kernel with a bandwidth <math>h</math> such that <math>K(\cdot)</math> is of order at least 1, that is <math>\int_{-\infty}^\infty u K(u) \, du = 0</math>.

=== Derivation ===

Starting with the definition of [[conditional expectation]],
: <math>
\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X=x) = \int y f(y\mid x) \, dy = \int y \frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)} \, dy
</math>

we estimate the joint distributions ''f''(''x'',''y'') and ''f''(''x'') using [[kernel density estimation]] with a kernel '''''K''''':

: <math>
\hat{f}(x,y) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i) K_h(y-y_i),
</math>
: <math>
\hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i),
</math>

We get:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{\hat E}(Y \mid X=x) &= \int y \frac{\hat{f}(x,y)}{\hat{f}(x)} \, dy,\\[6pt]
&= \int y \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i) K_h(y-y_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n K_h(x-x_j)} \,dy,\\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i) \int y \, K_h(y-y_i) \,dy}{\sum_{j=1}^n K_h(x-x_j)},\\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K_h(x-x_i) y_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n K_h(x-x_j)},
\end{align}
</math>

which is the Nadaraya–Watson estimator.

== Priestley–Chao kernel estimator ==
: <math>
\widehat{m}_{PC}(x) = h^{-1} \sum_{i=2}^n (x_i - x_{i-1}) K\left(\frac{x-x_i}{h}\right) y_i
</math>

where <math> h </math> is the bandwidth (or smoothing parameter).

== Gasser–Müller kernel estimator ==
: <math>
\widehat{m}_{GM}(x) = h^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i} K\left(\frac{x-u}{h}\right) \, du\right] y_i
</math>

where <math>s_i = \frac{x_{i-1} + x_i}{2}.</math><ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Gasser | first1 = Theo
 | last2 = Müller | first2 = Hans-Georg
 | contribution = Kernel estimation of regression functions
 | isbn = 3-540-09706-6
 | mr = 564251
 | pages = 23–68
 | publisher = Springer, Berlin
 | series = Lecture Notes in Math.
 | title = Smoothing techniques for curve estimation (Proc. Workshop, Heidelberg, 1979)
 | volume = 757
 | year = 1979}}</ref>

== Example ==
[[File:cps71 lc mean.png|thumb|right|250px|Estimated regression function.]]

This example is based upon Canadian cross-section wage data consisting of a random sample taken from the 1971 Canadian Census Public Use Tapes for male individuals having common education (grade 13). There are 205 observations in total.{{cn|date=September 2023}}

The figure to the right shows the estimated regression function using a second order Gaussian kernel along with asymptotic variability bounds.
{{clear}}

=== Script for example ===

The following commands of the [[R programming language]] use the <code>npreg()</code> function to deliver optimal smoothing and to create the figure given above. These commands can be entered at the command prompt via cut and paste.

<syntaxhighlight lang="r">
install.packages("np")
library(np) # non parametric library
data(cps71)
attach(cps71)

m <- npreg(logwage~age)

plot(m, plot.errors.method="asymptotic",
     plot.errors.style="band",
     ylim=c(11, 15.2))

points(age, logwage, cex=.25)
detach(cps71)
</syntaxhighlight>

== Related ==
According to [[David Salsburg]], the algorithms used in kernel regression were independently developed and used in [[fuzzy system]]s: "Coming up with almost exactly the same computer algorithm, fuzzy systems and kernel density-based regressions appear to have been developed completely independently of one another."<ref>{{cite book |last=Salsburg |first=D. |title=[[The Lady Tasting Tea|The Lady Tasting Tea: How Statistics Revolutionized Science in the Twentieth Century]] |publisher=W.H. Freeman |year=2002 |isbn=0-8050-7134-2 |pages=290–91 }}</ref>

== Statistical implementation ==
* [[GNU Octave]] mathematical program package
* [[Julia_(programming_language) | Julia]]: [https://github.com/panlanfeng/KernelEstimator.jl KernelEstimator.jl]
* [[MATLAB]]: A free MATLAB toolbox with implementation of kernel regression, kernel density estimation, kernel estimation of hazard function and many others is available on [https://www.math.muni.cz/english/science-and-research/developed-software/232-matlab-toolbox.html these pages] (this toolbox is a part of the book <ref name="HorKolZel">{{cite book|last1=Horová|first1=I.|last2=Koláček|first2=J.|last3=Zelinka|first3=J.|title=Kernel Smoothing in MATLAB: Theory and Practice of Kernel Smoothing|url=https://archive.org/details/kernelsmoothingi0000horo|date=2012|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|location=Singapore|isbn=978-981-4405-48-5}}</ref>).
* [[Python (programming language)|Python]]: the <code>[http://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.nonparametric.kernel_regression.KernelReg.html KernelReg]</code> class for mixed data types in the <code>[http://www.statsmodels.org/stable/nonparametric.html statsmodels.nonparametric]</code> sub-package (includes other kernel density related classes), the package [https://github.com/jmetzen/kernel_regression kernel_regression] as an extension of [[scikit-learn]] (inefficient memory-wise, useful only for small datasets)
* [[R (programming language)|R]]: the function <code>npreg</code> of the ''np'' package can perform kernel regression.<ref>[https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/np/index.html ''np'': Nonparametric kernel smoothing methods for mixed data types]</ref><ref>{{Cite book |first1=John |last1=Kloke |first2=Joseph W. |last2=McKean |title=Nonparametric Statistical Methods Using R |publisher=CRC Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4398-7343-4 |pages=98–106 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b-msBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA98 }}</ref>
* [[Stata]]: [https://web.archive.org/web/20180519032545/https://www.stata.com/manuals/rnpregress.pdf npregress], [https://ideas.repec.org/c/boc/bocode/s372601.html kernreg2]
